## Target Venue
- Primary: EMNLP 2026 Main (ARR submission)
- Deadline: 2026-05-25 (ARR May cycle)
- Track: LLM Security / Discourse and Pragmatics
- Commitment deadline: 2026-08-02

Persuasion classification is "compatible" (doesn't hurt) but not additive (doesn't help vs MLM). The persuasion taxonomy's sole surviving value is interpretability via strategy trajectory analysis. - Classification structure → Full/K≥3 robustness (scrambled/binary/9-class all Δ=0)
- Label granularity → K=2 bonus (9-class Δ=0 > scrambled Δ=-0.026 > binary Δ=-0.026)
- Label correctness → K=1 bonus (9-class Δ=-0.026 > scrambled Δ=-0.053 > binary Δ=-0.092 = MLM Δ=-0.092)
This resolves the "cannot attribute" caveat in experiments.tex and strengthens 9-class value beyond interpretability.

NOT: "Persuasion-aware fine-tuning is the critical ingredient" (MLM control falsified this — D019).
NOT: "An evasion hierarchy exists: lexical < semantic < pragmatic" (TF-IDF=0.94 on DD contradicts this).
YES: "We systematically decompose what makes multi-turn jailbreaks detectable across attack types. The surprising finding: domain-adaptive pretraining on jailbreak conversation text (even MLM) is sufficient for cross-attack generalization. Classification supervision, label quality, label granularity, temporal modeling, and loss weighting are all non-factors. Misaligned classification (topic) actively hurts (-37pp vs MLM). This pinpoints domain exposure as the mechanism and positions the persuasion taxonomy as an interpretability tool, not a detection driver."

## Title (Working)
What Makes Multi-Turn Jailbreaks Detectable? A Systematic Decomposition of Cross-Attack Generalization

## Core Insight (D030 — post-ActorAttack universal DA reframe)
Domain adaptation universally improves cross-attack generalization across encoder architectures; encoder pretraining determines the difficulty threshold at which adaptation becomes critical. Systematic ablation across two encoders (DeBERTa-v3, RoBERTa) and three OOD attack families (DD, FITD, ActorAttack) reveals:

**On Deceptive Delight (moderate OOD)**: DeBERTa vanilla collapses (F1=0.31±0.03), continued pretraining bridges ~60pp (MLM=0.91±0.12), classification achieves 0.997±0.005. RoBERTa vanilla already succeeds (0.981±0.026) — hierarchy is flat. Scrambled=binary=9-class (all 0.997±0.005).

**On ActorAttack (hard OOD)**: RoBERTa vanilla ALSO collapses (0.466±0.163), proving "no DA needed" was DD-specific. DeBERTa vanilla=0.258±0.000. Both encoders benefit from DA: DeBERTa 9-class=0.972±0.026, RoBERTa 9-class=0.939±0.046. Critically, scrambled (0.931) < 9-class (0.972) < binary (0.995) — label quality matters on hard attacks (DD ceiling effect had masked this).

**Cross-encoder CKA (D029)**: Both MLM and 9-class reshape representations substantially (centered CKA < 0.5 vs vanilla), but representation change magnitude ≠ detection improvement. RoBERTa MLM changes more (CKA=0.393) yet gains only 0.6pp; DeBERTa MLM changes less (CKA=0.442) yet gains 60pp. The starting point determines the return on adaptation.

**Key nuances**: (1) Binary > 9-class on ActorAttack (0.995 vs 0.972) — coarse labels more robust to structural OOD; fine-grained strategies may overfit training attack structure. (2) Classification supervision consistently reduces cross-seed variance to ~0.005 across both encoders. (3) OOD perturbation: 9-class vs vanilla p<0.001 (n=118), three-layer robustness attribution confirmed as observed pattern.

## Novelty Positioning (D030 reframe)
NOT: "Persuasion-aware fine-tuning is the critical ingredient" (MLM control falsified this on DD).
NOT: "RoBERTa doesn't need domain adaptation" (ActorAttack falsified this — D030).
NOT: "Label quality is irrelevant" (ActorAttack showed scrambled < 9-class < binary).
YES: "We systematically decompose cross-attack generalization across two encoder architectures and three OOD attack families. The key finding: domain adaptation universally improves generalization, but the benefit depends on encoder pretraining × attack structural complexity. On moderate OOD (DD), RoBERTa succeeds without adaptation while DeBERTa requires it; on structurally complex attacks (ActorAttack), both encoders require adaptation. Classification supervision provides complementary benefits: seed stability, perturbation robustness, and interpretability. Label quality becomes important only on hard OOD attacks — a finding masked by ceiling effects on easier benchmarks."

\begin{abstract}
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across seemingly benign conversational turns, evading per-turn safety filters.
We present preliminary findings from a systematic ablation on two encoder architectures that decomposes what enables cross-attack generalization in multi-turn jailbreak detection.
On DeBERTa-v3, continued pretraining is the primary mechanism: masked language modeling without labels bridges $\sim$60 percentage points (pp) of the out-of-distribution (OOD) gap (vanilla F1\,=\,0.31$\pm$0.03 $\to$ 0.91$\pm$0.12 on unseen attack types).
Cross-encoder validation on RoBERTa shows that domain adaptation is universally beneficial: RoBERTa vanilla achieves F1\,=\,0.981 on structurally simple Deceptive Delight but collapses to 0.466 on multi-persona ActorAttack, while domain-adapted variants maintain F1\,$\geq$\,0.93 on both.
Across both encoders, classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance to near-zero (std 0.005) and provides perturbation robustness on DeBERTa (zero degradation at full conversation length vs.\ $\sim$12\,pp for non-adapted models, $n$=76).
These results on synthetic conversations from four attack families suggest that domain adaptation universally improves cross-attack generalization, with encoder pretraining method determining the difficulty threshold at which adaptation becomes critical; validation on larger, human-generated datasets is needed.
\end{abstract}

% abstract.tex — cross-encoder revision
\begin{abstract}
Multi-turn jailbreak attacks distribute adversarial intent across seemingly benign conversational turns, evading per-turn safety filters.
We present preliminary findings from a systematic ablation on two encoder architectures that decomposes what enables cross-attack generalization in multi-turn jailbreak detection.
On DeBERTa-v3, continued pretraining is the primary mechanism: masked language modeling without labels bridges $\sim$60 percentage points (pp) of the out-of-distribution (OOD) gap (vanilla F1\,=\,0.31$\pm$0.03 $\to$ 0.91$\pm$0.12 on unseen attack types).
Cross-encoder validation on RoBERTa shows that domain adaptation is universally beneficial: RoBERTa vanilla achieves F1\,=\,0.981 on structurally simple Deceptive Delight but collapses to 0.466 on multi-persona ActorAttack, while domain-adapted variants maintain F1\,$\geq$\,0.93 on both.
Across both encoders, classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance to near-zero (std 0.005) and provides perturbation robustness on DeBERTa (zero degradation at full conversation length vs.\ $\sim$12\,pp for non-adapted models, $n$=76).
These results on synthetic conversations from four attack families suggest that domain adaptation universally improves cross-attack generalization, with encoder pretraining method determining the difficulty threshold at which adaptation becomes critical; validation on larger, human-generated datasets is needed.
\end{abstract}

% introduction.tex — expanded for 8-page target

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Multi-turn jailbreak attacks pose a qualitatively different threat to large language model (LLM) safety than their single-turn counterparts. Attacks such as Crescendo~\citep{russinovich2024crescendo}, Foot-in-the-Door (FITD)~\citep{fitd2024}, and Deceptive Delight~\citep{deceptivedelight2024} distribute adversarial intent across individually benign turns through rapport building, logical reframing, and incremental escalation. Persuasion is the common mechanism: \citet{zeng2024pap} catalogue 40 persuasion techniques across jailbreak families, and \citet{hagendorff2026reasoning} find identifiable strategies in 97\% of successful attacks. Individual attack turns occupy the same embedding region as benign text~\citep{bullwinkel2025repeng}, rendering per-turn safety filters fundamentally blind.

Production classifiers such as Llama Guard~\citep{inan2023llamaguard}, WildGuard~\citep{han2024wildguard}, and ShieldGemma~\citep{zeng2024shieldgemma} operate on individual turns and cannot model manipulation trajectories across exchanges. Recent multi-turn defenses have begun to address conversation-level structure: DeepContext~\citep{deepcontext2026} combines fine-tuned BERT with a multi-layer GRU, BIID~\citep{tong2025biid} infers turn-level intentions, and G-Guard~\citep{gguard2025} applies graph neural networks. These systems achieve reasonable in-distribution performance but are evaluated on single attack families and do not assess cross-dataset OOD transfer. None systematically analyze \emph{why} some representations generalize while others fail. The open question is: \emph{what representation properties enable cross-attack generalization?}

A vanilla DeBERTa encoder~\citep{he2021deberta} with temporal aggregation collapses from F1\,=\,1.000 on in-distribution data to F1\,=\,0.312$\pm$0.026 on out-of-distribution (OOD) Deceptive Delight, worsening with more turns (0.628 at turn~1 to 0.312 at full conversation). LLM-as-judge approaches fare no better: GPT-5.5 achieves F1 of only 0.191--0.449 on in-distribution detection with 30--47\% unparseable responses (Appendix~\ref{sec:llm_judge}). Content-level reasoning is insufficient for this task.

We built \textbf{DisPeD} (Discourse-level Persuasion Detection), a two-stage framework with seven controlled Stage~1 variants that systematically decompose the mechanism: 9-class persuasion strategy classification, binary classification, scrambled labels, MLM only, topic classification, Wikipedia MLM, and vanilla control (Section~\ref{sec:method}). Each variant isolates a specific factor (domain exposure, classification supervision, label quality, label granularity, or domain specificity) while holding all other components constant.

Through this systematic ablation on DeBERTa-v3, we find that domain exposure via continued pretraining bridges $\sim$60 percentage points (pp) of the OOD gap (vanilla 0.31$\pm$0.03 $\to$ MLM 0.91$\pm$0.12), with strong early detection on unseen Deceptive Delight (mean F1\,$\geq$\,0.97 at $K \leq 5$). Classification supervision provides complementary stability: the 9-class model achieves F1\,=\,0.997$\pm$0.005 with near-zero variance at full conversation length. Cross-encoder validation on RoBERTa~\citep{liu2019roberta} shows that domain adaptation is universally beneficial: RoBERTa vanilla achieves F1\,=\,0.981 on Deceptive Delight but collapses to 0.466$\pm$0.163 on structurally distinct ActorAttack~\citep{ren2024actorattack}, while domain-adapted variants maintain F1\,$\geq$\,0.93 on both. Encoder pretraining method determines the difficulty threshold at which adaptation becomes critical: DeBERTa-v3's replaced token detection (RTD)~\citep{he2021deberta} requires adaptation even for simple attacks, while RoBERTa's standard MLM pretraining tolerates simple attacks but fails on structurally complex ones. Across both encoders, classification supervision reduces cross-seed variance to 0.005--0.046.

Our contributions on this preliminary study of synthetic multi-turn jailbreak conversations:
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=*, itemsep=2pt, topsep=4pt]
  \item \textbf{Systematic decomposition.} Seven controlled DeBERTa-v3 variants identify continued pretraining as the primary mechanism for cross-attack generalization on this encoder ($\sim$60\,pp OOD gap bridged by MLM alone). Misaligned supervision (topic classification) actively destabilizes representations.

  \item \textbf{Cross-encoder validation.} Domain adaptation is universally beneficial: RoBERTa vanilla achieves F1\,=\,0.981 on Deceptive Delight but collapses to 0.466 on ActorAttack. Encoder pretraining method determines the difficulty threshold at which adaptation becomes critical (Section~\ref{sec:cross_encoder}).

  \item \textbf{Complementary role of classification supervision.} Classification adds perturbation robustness (zero degradation at full length on DeBERTa, $n$=76) and interpretable characterization of known attack families, though strategy predictions do not transfer to unseen attacks (Section~\ref{sec:strategy}).

  \item \textbf{Three-layer robustness attribution.} Under adversarial paraphrasing on DeBERTa, classification structure suffices at full length; correct and fine-grained labels are jointly required at $K$=2; both properties contribute independently at $K$=1.
\end{itemize}
